name: Battle of Marathon
info: The Athenians, helped by Plataea, defeated a Persian force under Datis and Artaphernes on the plain of Marathon in Attica in 490 BCE, ending the first Persian invasion of Greece.

facts.date: 12 September 490 BCE in the Julian calendar, the conventional date calculated by August Böckh in 1855; if the Spartan calendar was a month ahead of the Athenian, 12 August 490 BCE
facts.place: The plain and bay of Marathon, about 27 kilometres north-east of Athens in Attica, Greece
facts.sides: Athens under ten generals, with the war archon Callimachus, and Miltiades as the general most experienced against the Persians, with 1,000 Plataeans; ancient writers give 9,000 or 10,000 Athenians. The Persians under Datis and Artaphernes, for whom modern estimates run from 20,000 to 100,000 infantry, with a consensus of perhaps 25,000, and about 1,000 cavalry
facts.outcome: The Athenian and Plataean wings broke the Persian wings and then turned on the centre; the Persians fled to their ships and returned to Asia. Herodotus counted 6,400 Persian dead and 192 Athenian.

t: The Athenians fought without the Spartans, who had sent word that a religious festival kept them at home, and the Spartan army arrived only the day after the battle.

Herodotus gives no figure for the Athenian army and none for the Persian; ancient writers' numbers for the Persians range from 200,000 to 600,000, and modern historians put the infantry at perhaps 25,000.
The story of a runner carrying the news from Marathon to Athens first appears centuries after the battle; Herodotus's runner went from Athens to Sparta before it.
dyk: The modern marathon race comes from the legend of a runner from Marathon to Athens, which is not in Herodotus; the idea was proposed by Michel Bréal for the first modern Olympic Games in 1896.
ev: The Ionian cities revolt against Persian rule, and Athens and Eretria send a force that burns the lower city of Sardis
The Persian naval victory at Lade all but ends the Ionian Revolt
Datis and Artaphernes cross the Aegean, subdue the Cyclades and besiege and burn Eretria
The Persians land at Marathon and the Athenians block the two exits from the plain
After about five days of stalemate the Athenians attack and break the Persian wings, then the centre
The Persian fleet turns back from Athens after the Athenian army returns by forced march
Darius's Egyptian subjects revolt, postponing a new expedition against Greece
Xerxes I begins the second Persian invasion of Greece

sections.background:
The first Persian invasion of Greece grew from the Ionian Revolt. In 499 BCE the Ionian cities rose against Persian rule, and Athens and Eretria sent a force that marched to Sardis and burned the lower city before Persian horsemen drove it back to the coast with many losses. Darius I vowed to punish both cities; according to Herodotus he shot an arrow upwards and asked Zeus for vengeance on the Athenians, and had a servant remind him of them three times before dinner each day. The Persian victory at Lade in 494 BCE all but ended the revolt.

Athens had its own reasons for enmity with Persia. After the tyrant Hippias was expelled in 510 BCE, he fled to the Persian satrap Artaphernes at Sardis and promised the Persians control of Athens if they restored him. The Athenians, who had reformed their state under Cleisthenes, would not take him back, and went to open war with Persia. Darius meanwhile was extending his empire into Europe, having subdued Thrace and made Macedon a vassal.

In 492 BCE Darius sent his son-in-law Mardonius to Greece, but a storm wrecked the fleet. In 490 BCE he sent a naval expedition under Artaphernes, the satrap's son, and Datis, a Median admiral, to bring the Cyclades into the empire and then force Eretria and Athens to submit or be destroyed. After taking Naxos the force reached Euboea in mid-summer, besieged and burned Eretria, and sailed south to Attica on Hippias's advice.
sections.forces:
Herodotus gives no figure for the Athenian army. Cornelius Nepos, Pausanias and Plutarch give 9,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans, and Justin 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans; these figures are close to those Herodotus gives for Plataea eleven years later, and modern historians generally accept them as reasonable. Attica then had a population of about 315,000 including slaves, so the army was about 3 per cent of it. There were ten generals, one elected by each tribe, among them Miltiades, and the war archon Callimachus was in overall command.

Herodotus says the fleet had 600 triremes but does not estimate the army, describing only a large, well packed infantry. Simonides, a near contemporary, gives 200,000 for the expedition. Later writers give 200,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry (Nepos, who says only 100,000 fought), 300,000 (Plutarch, Pausanias and the Suda), 500,000 (Plato and Lysias) and 600,000 (Justin). Modern historians propose from 20,000 to 100,000 infantry, with a consensus of perhaps 25,000, and about 1,000 cavalry. Herodotus names the Persians and the Sakae at the centre of the line.

The Athenians held a strong position on a spur of Mount Agrieliki beside the plain, and blocked both exits. They were probably outnumbered at least two to one, had stripped Athens of defenders, and could not afford defeat. Hoplites were vulnerable to cavalry, and the Persian force contained many missile troops, lightly armoured and no match for hoplites in melee. Time favoured the Athenians, because every day brought the Spartans nearer.
sections.course:
The armies faced each other for about five days. Pheidippides, sent to Sparta for help, found the Spartans at the festival of Carneia and was told that they could not march until the full moon. The Greeks attacked before the Spartans came. One theory is that the Persian cavalry had left, perhaps being re-embarked to sail round Cape Sounion against Athens, and that the Athenians moved to exploit it; the other is that the Persians advanced and the Athenians then took the offensive. Neither can be firmly established; both may be true.

The armies stood about 1,500 metres apart. Miltiades ordered the Leontis tribe under Themistocles and the Antiochis tribe under Aristides to form the centre only four ranks deep, and the other tribes on the flanks eight deep. Some modern commentators see a plan for envelopment; others think the Greeks lacked the training for it and thinned the centre so that their line would match the Persian line in length. The Athenians advanced, probably walking until they reached the range of the archers, about 200 metres, and then running through the arrows; Herodotus says the Persians thought this madness.

Herodotus says the Persians and Sakae in the centre prevailed and pursued the Greeks inland, but on each wing the Athenians and Plataeans won. They let the routed wing troops flee and brought the wings together against the men who had broken through the centre. The Persians broke towards their ships, and some ran into the swamps, where an unknown number drowned. The Athenians followed them to the shore and captured seven ships, though most got away.
sections.aftermath:
Herodotus records that 6,400 Persian bodies were counted on the field, and it is unknown how many more died in the swamps. He reports that the Athenians lost 192 men, among them the war archon Callimachus and the general Stesilaos; he does not say how many Plataeans were killed. The dead of Athens and Plataea were buried on the battlefield in two mounds, and an epigram by Simonides was written on the Athenian tomb.

Herodotus says the Persian fleet then sailed round Cape Sounion to attack Athens directly, while some modern historians place that attempt just before the battle. Either way, the Athenian army marched back about 40 kilometres at great speed and arrived, he says, late in the afternoon, in time to prevent a landing, and the Persians turned back to Asia. The two tribes of the centre stayed to guard the field under Aristides. Herodotus also records a rumour that the move had been arranged with the Alcmaeonid family and that a shield signal was given; it cannot be told whether this was true.

The Spartan army arrived the next day, having covered 220 kilometres in three days, toured the battlefield and agreed that the Athenians had won a great victory. Darius began raising a larger army, but in 486 BCE Egypt revolted and he died while preparing to march there. His son Xerxes I put down the revolt and restarted preparations; the second invasion began in 480 BCE.
sections.sources:
The main source for the Greco-Persian Wars is Herodotus, born in 484 BCE at Halicarnassus, then under Persian rule, who wrote his Histories around 440 to 430 BCE. Thucydides began his own history where Herodotus stopped, and Plutarch accused Herodotus in an essay of being a lover of barbarians. His reputation has been rehabilitated since the 19th century by archaeological finds, although the prevailing view is that his troop numbers and dates should be treated with scepticism, and some historians think he invented much of his story. Diodorus Siculus, Plutarch, Ctesias and others add detail, and the Serpent Column supports some of Herodotus's claims.

No source gives the course of the battle in detail, and the surviving account is Greek. Historians dispute why the battle began when it did: Herodotus's story that the generals commanded in rotation and that Miltiades waited for his own day is called problematic, since there is little evidence for such a rotation. They also dispute the dates, since the lunisolar calendar dates of Herodotus depend on when the Spartans held their festival, and the conventional 12 September could be a month early.

The numbers are the most doubtful part. The ancient Persian figures run to many times the modern ones. Whether the Athenians planned an envelopment, and whether the Persian cavalry was present at all, are also disputed, as is the cause of the Greek success: most scholars point to better equipment and tactics, while Lazenby thought it rested on the courage of ordinary amateur soldiers.
sections.legacy:
For the Persian empire the defeat barely touched its vast resources, but for the Greeks it was the first time they had beaten the Persians. It showed that resistance was possible, that the Persians could be beaten, and that Athens could win without Sparta, which was regarded as the major military power. Militarily, it was the first time a hoplite phalanx faced mainly lightly armed troops, and it revealed how effective hoplites could be, although the phalanx remained vulnerable to cavalry.

In later centuries the battle came to be seen as a defining moment for the young Athenian democracy and the start of a golden age. John Stuart Mill held that Marathon was more important, even as an event in British history, than the Battle of Hastings. Aeschylus, who fought there, is said to have thought it his greatest achievement, for his gravestone names Marathon and not his plays.

Legends gathered round it: Pan, who was said to have frightened the Persians, the phantom of Theseus, a rustic with a plough who was honoured as a hero, and a vow to sacrifice as many goats as there were Persians slain, so that 500 were offered yearly. The runner who dies after announcing the victory is first told by Plutarch in the 1st century CE, citing Heracleides of Pontus. Michel Bréal proposed a marathon race for the first modern Olympics in 1896, and its distance was fixed at 42.195 kilometres.

summary: At Marathon in 490 BCE the Athenians and Plataeans attacked a Persian force sent by Darius I, broke its wings and drove it to the ships. Herodotus counted 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead. The first Persian invasion of Greece ended, and a second came in 480 BCE.
notes: Nepos's figure is given as the article gives it: 200,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry, of whom only 100,000 fought. Simonides is called a near-contemporary by the article.
The article gives no casualty figure for the Persians beyond Herodotus's 6,400 plus an unknown number in the swamps, and none for the Plataeans.
The article says the Athenian army 'arrived back in the late afternoon' on Herodotus's account; I attribute it to him.
The article reports the Persian re-embarkation theory (cavalry leaving) from the Suda entry; I gave the two theories briefly and did not quote the Suda.
Left out: Cynaegirus's hand, the epigram texts, Asimov's what-if view, Vic Hurley's view, Hippias's role in the choice of landing beyond one clause, the Plataea muster story and the tale of the dog.
Date: the article gives 12 September 490 BCE (Böckh, 1855), conventionally accepted, or 12 August if the Spartan calendar was a month ahead; I give both.
The article's own phrase for the Persian wings is 'inferior Persian levies'; I did not use it, to avoid taking a side beyond Herodotus.
